To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
5-9 % of young women with early-on-set breast cancer may have a TP53 mutation, even if they do not have a family history of cancer, and that testing for mutations in TP53 may be beneficial.

1) TP53 testing is underutilized in young women with breast cancer; 2) TP53 testing in young women with early-on-set breast cancer should be considered; and 3) TP53 testing may be considered in young women with negative BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 test results.

(a) 5-8 % of women diagnosed with breast cancers under age 30 have a mutation in a gene that is not routinely tested for (TP53); and (b) routine genetic testing of the three most common breast cancer genes (BRCA 1/2/3) in women with early-onse breast cancer is safe, and may be cost-effective, compared to testing only BRCA1 and 2

the potential for TP53 testing to be expanded to include women with early-onse breast cancer who have a negative or uncertain family history.
the identification of women with a germline TP53 mutation who do not meet current criteria of Li-Fraumenie syndrome.
a small subset of women with early-on-set breast cancer who may have a mutation that is missed by traditional genetic testing.
